# .NET Made Easy

> A free, written C# and .NET course from Layerbit: 315 lessons in three tiers, from a first program to running .NET in production. No signup and no paywall.

Every lesson is a standalone HTML page with a plain-English explanation, diagrams, C# code examples, common mistakes and a short quiz. The course targets C# 14 and .NET 10.

## Start here

- [Start Here guide](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/start-here.html): which path to take and a week-by-week plan for beginners and for developers switching to C#
- [.NET developer roadmap](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/dotnet-developer-roadmap.html): the skills a .NET developer needs, in order, each linked to its lessons
- [All lessons](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/lessons.html): the full syllabus with reading times
- [C# interview questions](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/interview-prep.html): common C# and .NET interview questions with direct answers
- [C# cheat sheet](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/csharp-cheatsheet.html): everyday C# syntax on one page
- [C# and .NET glossary](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/glossary.html): plain-English definitions of .NET terms
- [Interactive course player](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/): the same lessons with progress tracking and search

## C# Foundations

### Part I — C# and .NET

- [What Are C# and .NET? A Plain-English Introduction](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/003-what-are-c-and-net.html): What C# is, what .NET is, and how the language, the CLR runtime and the libraries fit together, plus when C# and .NET are the right choice for a project.
- [Install .NET 10 and Set Up Your C# Development Environment](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/004-setting-up-the-modern-environment.html): Install the .NET 10 SDK, choose VS Code or Visual Studio, and see what dotnet run actually does. Covers SDK vs runtime and the layout of a new project.
- [Your First C# Program: Create, Build and Run It Step by Step](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/005-your-first-c-application.html): Create, build and run your first C# console app with the .NET CLI, then read every line of the code and the .csproj file. Covers dotnet run vs dotnet build.

### Part II — Language Fundamentals

- [C# Variables and Constants: var, const and readonly Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/007-variables-and-constants.html): How C# variables and constants store data, when to use var or an explicit type, and the real difference between const and readonly, with simple examples.
- [C# Data Types: int, double, decimal, bool, char and More](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/008-built-in-data-types.html): A complete tour of C#'s built-in data types with a reference table, plus float vs double vs decimal and when implicit typing with var is the right call.
- [C# Strings: Working With Text, StringBuilder and Equality](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/009-strings-and-text.html): How C# strings work and why they never change. Covers StringBuilder, == vs Equals, null vs empty vs whitespace, char vs string, and spans for fast text.
- [C# Type Conversion: Casting, Parse, TryParse and Convert](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/010-type-conversion.html): Convert between types in C# safely: implicit vs explicit casts, Convert vs Parse vs TryParse, the as operator, boxing, and culture-aware number parsing.
- [C# Operators Explained: Arithmetic, Comparison and Logical](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/011-operators.html): Every everyday C# operator with examples: arithmetic, comparison, logical and ternary. Covers = vs ==, && vs &, integer division and operator precedence.
- [C# Control Flow: if, switch, for, foreach and while Loops](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/012-control-flow.html): Make decisions and repeat work in C# with if/else, switch, for, foreach, while and do-while. Includes break vs continue and switch statement vs expression.
- [C# Methods: Parameters, Return Values and Overloading](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/013-methods.html): Write reusable C# methods: parameters vs arguments, return types and void, static vs instance methods, pass by value vs by reference, and overloading.

### Part III — Object-Oriented C#

- [C# Classes and Objects Explained for Beginners](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/015-classes-and-objects.html): How C# classes act as blueprints and objects as the real instances, with fields, properties and methods. Covers class vs struct and when to use records.
- [C# Fields vs Properties: Getters, Setters and Auto-Properties](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/016-fields-and-properties.html): Fields store data and properties control access to it. Learn C# get and set accessors, auto-properties, private setters, and why public fields cause trouble.
- [C# Constructors: Default, Chained and Primary Constructors](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/017-constructors.html): How C# constructors set up new objects: default constructors, chaining with this() and base(), and how primary constructors compare to explicit ones.
- [C# Static Members: Static Fields, Methods and Constructors](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/018-static-members.html): Static members belong to the type, not to an instance. Learn when to use static fields, methods and constructors in C#, and what static code cannot access.
- [C# Access Modifiers: public, private, protected and internal](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/019-access-modifiers.html): Control who can use your C# types and members with public, private, protected and internal, plus protected internal, private protected and the defaults.
- [Encapsulation in C#: Hiding Data the Right Way](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/020-encapsulation.html): Encapsulation in C# explained with examples: why properties beat public fields, how it differs from abstraction, and what an object should keep private.
- [C# Value Types vs Reference Types Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/021-value-vs-reference-types.html): The difference between value types and reference types in C#: what gets copied, what gets shared, struct vs class, and what pass by value really means.
- [C# Structs: When to Use a Struct Instead of a Class](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/022-structs.html): What C# structs are, how they differ from classes, and when they make code faster. Clears up myths such as 'structs are always allocated on the stack'.
- [C# Enums Explained: Named Constants and [Flags]](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/023-enums.html): Use C# enums to give names to numbers and make code safer to read. Covers underlying values, the [Flags] attribute and the most common enum misconceptions.
- [C# Inheritance for Beginners: Base and Derived Classes](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/024-inheritance.html): Build new C# classes on top of existing ones with inheritance. Covers base and derived classes, virtual vs abstract vs override, and base constructors.
- [C# Polymorphism for Beginners: virtual and override](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/025-polymorphism.html): Polymorphism lets C# treat different objects through one base type or interface. Learn virtual, override and abstract, and when polymorphism really helps.
- [C# Method Overloading vs Overriding: The Difference](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/026-overloading-and-overriding.html): Overloading gives one method name several parameter lists. Overriding lets a derived class replace a base method. See both in C# with clear examples.
- [C# Interfaces for Beginners: Contracts Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/027-interfaces-first-look.html): A C# interface is a contract a class promises to fulfil. Learn how to declare and implement interfaces, and when to choose an interface or an abstract class.
- [Composition vs Inheritance in C#: When to Use Each](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/028-composition-vs-inheritance.html): 'Is-a' vs 'has-a': why C# developers often prefer composition over inheritance, the problems deep hierarchies cause, and how to choose between them.

### Part IV — Collections and Data

- [C# Arrays: Declare, Initialize and Loop Through Arrays](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/030-arrays.html): C# arrays hold a fixed number of same-typed values with instant index access. Learn to create and use them, and how an array differs from a List<T>.
- [C# Multidimensional Arrays: 2D Grids With int[,]](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/031-multidimensional-arrays.html): Store grids of data with C# multidimensional arrays. Learn the int[,] syntax, GetLength vs Length, and how rectangular arrays differ from jagged arrays.
- [C# Jagged Arrays: Arrays of Arrays Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/032-jagged-arrays.html): A jagged array in C# is an array of arrays where each row can have its own length. Learn the syntax, how it differs from int[,], and when to use one.
- [C# List<T> Explained: The Everyday Resizable Collection](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/033-lists.html): List<T> is the C# collection you will use most. Learn how it grows, how to add and remove items, and the difference between Count, Length and Capacity.
- [C# Dictionary<TKey,TValue>: Key/Value Lookups Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/034-dictionaries.html): Store key/value pairs in a C# Dictionary and find values almost instantly. Covers TryGetValue vs the indexer, ordering, and Dictionary vs a list of pairs.
- [C# HashSet<T>: Store Unique Values With Fast Lookups](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/035-hashset.html): A HashSet in C# keeps only unique values with dictionary-speed lookups. Learn when to use HashSet<T> instead of a List or a Dictionary, with examples.
- [C# Stack vs Queue: LIFO and FIFO Collections Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/036-stack-and-queue.html): Stack<T> gives back the last item added and Queue<T> the first. Learn Push, Pop, Enqueue and Dequeue in C#, and when each of the two collections fits.
- [C# Collection Interfaces: IEnumerable, ICollection, IList](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/037-collection-interfaces.html): The contracts every C# collection shares: IEnumerable<T>, ICollection<T>, IList<T> and the read-only versions, and which one to use as a parameter type.
- [IEnumerable<T> in C#: How foreach Really Works](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/038-ienumerable-t-first-look.html): IEnumerable<T> is the one promise every C# collection makes. Learn how foreach uses it, how it differs from IEnumerator<T>, and why it has no Count.

### Part V — Errors, Files and Dates

- [C# Exception Handling: try, catch and finally Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/040-exception-handling.html): Handle errors in C# with try, catch and finally. Learn the exception hierarchy, multiple catch blocks, and why exceptions beat easily ignored error codes.
- [C# Custom Exceptions: Creating and Throwing Errors](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/041-creating-and-throwing.html): Create your own exception types in C#, throw them correctly, and avoid the throw ex stack-trace trap. Also covers exception filters with the when keyword.
- [C# File and Directory Operations: Read and Write Files](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/042-file-and-directory-operations.html): Read, write and manage files and folders in C# with the File and Directory classes, and learn why async I/O matters once your code touches the disk.
- [C# File Paths: Path.Combine and Cross-Platform Paths](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/043-paths.html): Build file paths that work on Windows, Linux and macOS with Path.Combine and friends, and learn what a relative path is actually relative to in .NET.
- [C# Streams Explained: FileStream, StreamReader and using](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/044-streams-introduction.html): A stream is data flowing in or out, not a fixed pile. Learn FileStream vs StreamReader in C# and why using statements matter for releasing resources.
- [C# DateTime vs DateTimeOffset: Which One Should You Use?](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/045-datetime-and-datetimeoffset.html): DateTime vs DateTimeOffset in C#: why DateTime.Kind can't be trusted, why you should store UTC, and how DateTimeOffset records exactly when something happened.
- [C# Time Zones: Store UTC and Convert With TimeZoneInfo](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/046-time-zones.html): Handle time zones correctly in .NET: store UTC, convert to local time only for display with TimeZoneInfo, and avoid fixed offsets that break with DST.
- [Working With JSON in C#: System.Text.Json Basics](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/047-working-with-json.html): Serialize and deserialize JSON in C# with System.Text.Json, set the common options, and see why JSON became the shared language of web APIs.
- [C# Serialization Explained: Turning Objects Into Data](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/048-serialization.html): What serialization means in .NET, how JSON relates to it, which other formats such as XML exist, and how to choose a format for your C# application.

### Part VI — Modern C# Fundamentals

- [C# Nullable Reference Types: Catch Null Bugs at Compile Time](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/050-nullable-reference-types.html): Turn on nullable reference types in C# and let the compiler warn about null bugs before runtime. Covers string? vs string and nullable value types.
- [C# Null Handling: ?., ??, ??= and the ! Operator](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/051-null-safe-programming.html): Handle null cleanly in C# with the null-conditional ?. operator and null-coalescing ?? and ??=, and learn why the null-forgiving ! operator checks nothing.
- [C# Pattern Matching Explained With Examples](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/052-pattern-matching.html): Use C# pattern matching to test a value's type and shape in one expression: type, property, relational and logical patterns with is and switch.
- [C# Records Explained: record vs class and the with Expression](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/053-records-introduction.html): C# records compare by value, not by reference. Learn record vs class, how with creates modified copies, and why records are not automatically immutable.
- [C# Tuples and Deconstruction: Return Multiple Values](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/054-tuples-deconstruction.html): Return several values from a C# method with tuples, name the elements, and unpack them with deconstruction. Covers ValueTuple vs the old System.Tuple.
- [C# Switch Expressions: Modern switch With Examples](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/055-modern-switch-expressions.html): Switch expressions in C# produce a value instead of running statements. Learn the syntax, why the first matching arm wins, and exhaustiveness warnings.
- [C# Collection Expressions: The [ ] Syntax and Spread ..](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/056-modern-collection-expressions.html): Create arrays, lists and spans with one [ ] syntax in modern C#. Learn how collection expressions pick a target type and how the .. spread element works.
- [C# required Members: Mandatory Properties Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/057-required-members.html): The C# required modifier makes callers set key properties in an object initializer. Learn how it works with init, constructors and nullable types.
- [C# Primary Constructors for Classes and Structs](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/058-primary-constructors.html): Primary constructors put constructor parameters on the type declaration in C# 12 and later. Learn how they work and how they differ from positional records.

### Part VII — Practical Development

- [Debugging C# Code: Breakpoints, Step Into and Step Over](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/060-debugging-c-applications.html): Stop guessing and start inspecting. Learn to debug C# with breakpoints, Step Into vs Step Over, and variable inspection instead of print statements.
- [How to Read a C# Stack Trace and Find the Bug Fast](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/061-reading-stack-traces.html): A .NET stack trace is a map to the bug. Learn to read it line by line, why the top line isn't always the cause, and why throw; beats throw ex;.
- [Writing Clean C# Code: Practical Rules for Beginners](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/062-writing-clean-c.html): Write C# that other people can read: clear names, small methods and simple logic. Learn why clean does not mean clever, and short does not mean clear.
- [C# Naming Conventions: PascalCase, camelCase and _fields](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/063-naming-conventions.html): The standard .NET naming conventions in one table: PascalCase vs camelCase, the underscore prefix for private fields, and why Hungarian notation is out.
- [Common C# Beginner Mistakes and How to Avoid Them](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/064-common-beginner-mistakes.html): The mistakes almost every new C# developer makes, from value vs reference confusion and == vs Equals to a missing override and catching exceptions too broadly.
- [C# Beginner Project: Build an Expense Tracker Console App](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/065-project-expense-tracker.html): Build a complete C# console app that tracks expenses, using classes, collections, file storage and exception handling together. Full solution included.
- [C# OOP Project: Build an Employee Payroll System](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/066-project-employee-system.html): Practise C# inheritance and polymorphism by building a payroll system with different employee types and one shared contract. Full solution included.
- [C# Fundamentals Challenge: Test What You've Learned](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/067-fundamentals-challenge.html): Challenges covering the whole C# Foundations tier, from types and control flow to OOP and collections. Find out how much stuck before moving on.

## C# In Practice

### Part I — Advanced OOP

- [Object-Oriented Programming in C#: Beyond the Basics](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/070-oop-revisited.html): Revisit the four OOP pillars in C# with a working developer's eye: what changes when you build real systems with encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
- [Encapsulation in Real C# Applications: Rich Domain Models](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/071-encapsulation-in-real-applications.html): Real encapsulation protects the rules your objects must never break. Learn rich vs anemic domain models in C#, and how to encapsulate a collection safely.
- [C# Inheritance in Depth: The Fragile Base Class Problem](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/072-inheritance-2.html): What happens to C# inheritance in large codebases: the fragile base class problem, virtual, override and sealed override, and constructor chaining with base.
- [Composition in C#: Building Flexible, Testable Services](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/073-composition.html): Use composition as the structure of real C# services: compose small parts, apply the strategy shape, and build a notification service from components.
- [Polymorphism in Practice: Polymorphic Collections in C#](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/074-polymorphism-2.html): Put polymorphism to work in C#: polymorphic collections, the Liskov Substitution Principle, and one reporting engine built two ways to compare designs.
- [C# Abstract Classes: When to Use Them vs Interfaces](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/075-abstract-classes.html): An abstract class in C# shares implementation and enforces a contract. Learn abstract vs virtual methods and when to choose an abstract class or interface.
- [C# sealed Classes and Members: When and Why to Seal](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/076-sealed-classes-and-members.html): Use the C# sealed keyword to stop a class being inherited or a member being overridden further. Learn sealed override and when sealing is the right call.
- [C# Interfaces in Depth: Default Methods, DI and Testing](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/077-interfaces.html): Go deeper with C# interfaces: default interface methods, interfaces as team boundaries, and designing interfaces for dependency injection and unit tests.
- [Implementing Multiple Interfaces in C#](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/078-multiple-interface-implementation.html): One C# class can implement several interfaces to combine capabilities. Learn how to resolve member name conflicts and how this differs from inheritance.
- [Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) in C# With Examples](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/079-interface-segregation.html): The I in SOLID: no class should depend on methods it doesn't use. See how fat C# interfaces hurt, and split a bloated IRepository step by step.
- [C# Explicit Interface Implementation Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/080-explicit-interface-implementation.html): Use explicit interface implementation in C# when two interfaces clash or a member should only be reachable through the interface. Syntax and examples.
- [Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) in C# With Examples](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/081-dependency-inversion.html): The D in SOLID explained in C#: depend on abstractions, not concrete classes. Learn what gets inverted and apply DIP step by step to an order service.

### Part II — Generics & Collections

- [C# Generics Explained: Type-Safe Reusable Code](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/083-generics.html): Generics let one piece of C# code work with any type while keeping type safety. Learn the problem generics solve, what T means, and why they beat object.
- [C# Generic Classes: Writing Your Own Generic Types](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/084-generic-classes.html): Write your own generic classes in C#: one or more type parameters, how they flow through members, and using primary constructors with generic types.
- [C# Generic Methods: Type Parameters on a Single Method](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/085-generic-methods.html): A C# method can be generic on its own, even inside a non-generic class. Learn the syntax, type inference, and when to pass explicit type arguments.
- [C# Generic Constraints: Telling the Compiler What T Can Do](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/086-generic-constraints.html): Unconstrained T can do almost nothing. Learn how C# generic constraints unlock members on T, what they restrict, and why compiling for int proves little.
- [C# where Constraints: class, struct, new() and notnull](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/087-where-constraints.html): A practical guide to C# where constraints: class, struct, new(), notnull, base classes and interfaces, and how to pick exactly the one your code needs.
- [C# Covariance and Contravariance: in and out Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/088-covariance-and-contravariance.html): Why a List<Dog> is not a List<Animal> but an IEnumerable<Dog> is an IEnumerable<Animal>. Learn C# generic variance with the in and out keywords.
- [C# Generic Collections: List, Dictionary, SortedList and More](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/089-generic-collections.html): A guided tour of .NET's generic collections: List<T>, Dictionary, HashSet, SortedList vs SortedDictionary, LinkedList<T>, and how to choose one.
- [How a C# Dictionary Works Internally: Hashing and Buckets](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/090-dictionary-internals.html): Why a .NET Dictionary lookup is O(1): hash codes, buckets and collisions explained step by step, and why buckets don't preserve insertion order.
- [C# Equals and GetHashCode: Equality and Hashing Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/091-equality-and-hashing.html): Equals and GetHashCode form one contract in C#. Learn ReferenceEquals vs Equals vs ==, why equal hashes don't mean equal objects, and how to override both.
- [C# IComparable<T>: Sorting Your Own Types](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/092-icomparable-t.html): Teach List<T>.Sort() and Array.Sort() how to order your own C# types by implementing IComparable<T> and CompareTo, with examples and common pitfalls.
- [C# IEquatable<T>: Fast, Type-Safe Equality for Your Types](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/093-iequatable-t.html): Implement IEquatable<T> in C# for type-safe equality without boxing structs. Learn how Equals(T) relates to Equals(object) and why GetHashCode still matters.
- [Build a Custom Collection in C# With IEnumerable<T>](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/094-custom-collections.html): Build your own C# collection from scratch: implement IEnumerable<T> with yield return, and decide when implementing ICollection<T> is worth the effort.

### Part III — Delegates & Functional C#

- [C# Delegates Explained: Methods as Variables](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/096-delegates.html): A C# delegate is a variable that holds a method, so behaviour can be passed around like data. Learn how to declare, assign and invoke delegates.
- [C# Custom and Multicast Delegates Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/097-custom-delegates.html): Declare your own delegate types in C# and use multicast delegates to call a whole list of methods from one trigger, with += and -= explained precisely.
- [C# Action Delegate: Action, Action<T> and When to Use It](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/098-action.html): Action is the ready-made C# delegate for methods that return nothing. Learn Action and Action<T> with examples, and why you rarely need custom void delegates.
- [C# Func Delegate: Func<T, TResult> Explained With Examples](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/099-func.html): Func is the built-in C# delegate for methods that return a value, and the type behind most LINQ methods. Learn which type parameter is the return type.
- [C# Predicate<T> vs Func<T, bool>: What's the Difference?](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/100-predicate.html): Predicate<T> is a named C# delegate for testing a condition. Learn how it relates to Func<T, bool>, why both exist, and why you can't swap them freely.
- [C# Lambda Expressions: The => Syntax Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/101-lambda-expressions.html): A lambda in C# is a nameless method written inline with =>. Learn expression and statement lambdas, how they become delegates, and where you use them daily.
- [C# Closures Explained: Captured Variables and Loop Traps](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/102-closures.html): When a C# lambda captures an outside variable, it captures the variable itself, not a copy. Learn how closures work and avoid the classic loop variable trap.
- [C# Local Functions vs Lambdas: When to Use Each](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/103-local-functions.html): Local functions are named helpers inside a C# method. Learn how they differ from lambdas, why they suit recursion, and how they avoid delegate overhead.
- [Higher-Order Functions in C# With Func and Action](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/104-higher-order-functions.html): Higher-order functions take or return other functions. See how C# uses Func and Action to separate what varies from what stays the same, with examples.
- [C# Events Explained: The event Keyword and Subscribers](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/105-events.html): The C# event keyword wraps a delegate so subscribers can only add or remove themselves. Learn how events work and why a raw delegate field is unsafe.
- [C# Event Pattern: EventHandler, EventArgs and Memory Leaks](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/106-event-patterns.html): The standard .NET event pattern: EventHandler<T>, EventArgs, a protected raiser method, thread-safe raising, and the memory leak caused by not unsubscribing.
- [Event-Driven Design in C#: Decoupling With Events](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/107-event-driven-design.html): Use C# events to decouple an application: publish a fact and let other components react, without the publisher ever knowing who is listening.

### Part IV — LINQ

- [C# LINQ Tutorial for Beginners: Introduction to LINQ](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/109-introduction-to-linq.html): LINQ lets you query data in C# by saying what you want instead of writing loops. A beginner-friendly introduction to LINQ with before-and-after examples.
- [IEnumerable vs IQueryable in C#: The Key Difference](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/110-ienumerable-and-iqueryable.html): IEnumerable<T> runs a LINQ query in memory, while IQueryable<T> translates it to run somewhere else, such as a database. Learn when each one is used.
- [LINQ Where in C#: Filtering Collections With Examples](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/111-filtering.html): Filter C# collections with LINQ's Where, filter by type with OfType<T>, and use index-aware filtering. Also covers OfType vs Cast and chained Where calls.
- [LINQ Select and SelectMany in C#: Projection Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/112-projection.html): Reshape data with LINQ projection in C#: Select to transform each item and SelectMany to flatten nested collections into one sequence, with examples.
- [LINQ OrderBy and ThenBy in C#: Sorting Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/113-sorting.html): Sort sequences with LINQ's OrderBy, OrderByDescending and ThenBy in C#. Learn why OrderBy returns a new sequence and how it differs from List<T>.Sort().
- [LINQ GroupBy in C#: Grouping Data With Examples](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/114-grouping.html): Group items by key with LINQ GroupBy in C#. Learn IGrouping<TKey,TElement>, element and result selectors, and why grouping does not sort your data.
- [LINQ Join and GroupJoin in C#: Combining Collections](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/115-joining.html): Combine two collections on a shared key with LINQ Join, keep unmatched items with GroupJoin, and learn why LINQ's Join is always an equi-join.
- [LINQ Aggregation in C#: Count, Sum, Average, Min, Max](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/116-aggregation.html): Collapse a sequence to one value with LINQ's Count, Sum, Average, Min, Max and Aggregate in C#, and see how each one behaves on an empty sequence.
- [LINQ Deferred Execution in C#: When Queries Actually Run](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/117-deferred-execution.html): A LINQ query in C# doesn't run when you write it. Learn deferred execution, why queries re-run on every enumeration, and how captured variables surprise you.
- [LINQ Immediate Execution: ToList, ToArray and ToDictionary](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/118-immediate-execution.html): Force a LINQ query to run now with ToList, ToArray, ToDictionary and ToHashSet. Learn when immediate execution is the right choice, and ToList vs ToArray.
- [LINQ Query Syntax in C#: from, where, select and let](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/119-linq-query-syntax.html): Write LINQ in C# with SQL-like query syntax using from, where, select and let. Learn what query syntax can't express and why it is not actually SQL.

### Part VII — Async Programming

- [Synchronous vs Asynchronous Programming in C#](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/150-synchronous-vs-asynchronous.html): Why blocking threads wastes resources and how asynchronous C# code frees them. Learn what async really means and how it differs from multithreading.
- [Task and Task<T> in C#: Async Basics Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/151-task-and-task-t.html): A Task in C# is a handle for work that may not be finished yet. Learn Task vs Task<T>, how to get a result, and why a Task does not mean a new thread.
- [C# async and await Explained Step by Step](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/152-async-await.html): What async and await really do in C#: pause, free the thread, and resume when the result is ready. Learn the syntax, and why to go async all the way.
- [CancellationToken in C#: Cancel Async Operations Safely](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/153-cancellationtoken.html): Cancellation in .NET is cooperative. Learn to pass a CancellationToken, check it in async C# code, and why Cancel() never stops work immediately.
- [Task.WhenAll in C#: Run Async Tasks Concurrently](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/154-task-whenall.html): Run independent async operations at the same time with Task.WhenAll in C#, and learn how it collects every exception when more than one task fails.
- [Task.WhenAny in C#: Act on the First Task to Finish](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/155-task-whenany.html): Use Task.WhenAny in C# to react to whichever task finishes first, and remember that WhenAny never cancels the tasks that lose the race.
- [Exception Handling in Async C#: try/catch With await](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/156-exception-handling-in-async.html): How exceptions flow through async C# code: they are captured on the Task and rethrown at await. Covers try/catch around await and unobserved exceptions.
- [Async Streams in C#: IAsyncEnumerable and await foreach](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/157-async-streams.html): Async streams let C# consume values that arrive over time. Learn IAsyncEnumerable<T> and await foreach, and when a stream beats returning a whole list.
- [IAsyncEnumerable<T> in C#: Write Async Iterators](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/158-iasyncenumerable-t.html): Write your own async iterators in C# by combining yield return with await, including streaming paginated API results as each page arrives.
- [Common Async/Await Mistakes in C# and How to Fix Them](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/159-common-async-mistakes.html): Five async/await mistakes that compile fine but cause real bugs in C#, from async void to blocking on async code, with the fix for each one.

### Part I — Advanced C# Language

- [.NET Garbage Collection Explained: How the GC Works](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/172-garbage-collection.html): How the .NET garbage collector frees memory you never release yourself: reachability, why objects aren't freed instantly, and why .NET skips reference counting.

- [Boxing and Unboxing in C#: Hidden Costs Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/176-boxing-and-unboxing.html): Boxing wraps a C# value type in a heap object. Learn exactly when it happens, what it costs, and how ArrayList vs List<T> shows the difference.

- [Advanced C# Generics: How the CLR Shares Generic Code](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/180-advanced-generics.html): How .NET compiles generics: shared code for reference types, specialised code for value types, and why C# generics are not erased like Java generics.
- [Variance in C# and .NET: Array Covariance and Generic Rules](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/181-variance.html): Why string[] can pose as object[] in .NET and fail at runtime, and how generic variance with in and out avoids that by checking positions at compile time.

- [Race Conditions in C#: Why count++ Isn't Thread-Safe](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/217-race-conditions.html): A race condition gives different answers from the same input. Learn why count++ is several steps, how races happen in C#, and the two ways to prevent them.
- [Deadlocks in C#: Lock Ordering and Async Deadlocks](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/218-deadlocks.html): How deadlocks happen in C#: the classic two-lock ordering deadlock and the async deadlock, plus the discipline that prevents both of them.

### Part VI — Architecture & Design

- [Factory Pattern in C#: Simple Factory and Factory Method](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/240-factory-pattern.html): Let something other than the caller decide which class gets built. Learn the factory pattern family in C# with a notification sender selection example.
- [Strategy Pattern in C#: Swap Algorithms at Runtime](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/241-strategy-pattern.html): The strategy pattern in C# lets you swap an algorithm without changing the code that uses it. Shown in two forms with a shipping cost calculation.
- [Decorator Pattern in C#: Add Behavior Without Changing Code](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/242-decorator-pattern.html): Wrap an object to add logging or retries without touching the original class. Learn the decorator pattern in C# and how to stack several decorators.
- [Adapter Pattern in C#: Wrap Third-Party APIs Cleanly](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/243-adapter-pattern.html): The adapter pattern in C# lets your code see a third-party library through your own interface, so you can swap providers later. Explained with examples.
- [Observer Pattern in C#: From GoF to the event Keyword](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/244-observer-pattern.html): The observer pattern in C#: the classic Gang of Four shape, and how the event keyword maps onto subjects and observers in everyday .NET code.
- [Builder Pattern in C#: When You Still Need a Builder](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/245-builder-pattern.html): The builder pattern in C#: the telescoping constructor problem, how modern C# already covers most cases, and when a real builder still earns its keep.
- [Mediator Pattern in C#: Decouple Components With a Hub](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/246-mediator-pattern.html): The mediator pattern in C# routes communication through one object instead of many direct links, shown with a checkout dialog and request handlers.
- [Repository Pattern in C# With EF Core: A Practical Guide](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/247-repository-pattern.html): Build the repository pattern in C# on top of EF Core: what belongs inside a repository and what doesn't, with the trade-offs stated honestly.
- [Unit of Work Pattern in C# and EF Core](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/248-unit-of-work.html): The unit of work pattern groups changes into one commit. Learn why EF Core's DbContext already is one, and where a hand-rolled unit of work still helps.
- [Clean Architecture in .NET: Layers and the Dependency Rule](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/249-clean-architecture.html): Clean Architecture in .NET explained: the four rings, the dependency rule, and one product feature flowing through the domain, application and infrastructure.
- [Hexagonal Architecture in .NET: Ports and Adapters](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/250-hexagonal-architecture.html): Hexagonal architecture, also called ports and adapters, explained for .NET developers: the same dependency rule as Clean Architecture, drawn as a hexagon.
- [Domain-Driven Design (DDD) in C#: Core Concepts Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/251-domain-driven-design.html): The core ideas of Domain-Driven Design for C# developers, starting from ubiquitous language, explained in plain English with code examples.

### Part VII — Production ASP.NET

- [ASP.NET Core Architecture: Host, Kestrel and the Pipeline](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/253-asp-net-core-architecture.html): How ASP.NET Core is put together: the host, dependency injection and configuration you already know, plus the Kestrel web server and routing.
- [ASP.NET Core Middleware Explained: The Request Pipeline](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/254-middleware.html): Every ASP.NET Core request flows through a middleware pipeline and back out again. Learn why the order matters and how to write your own middleware.
- [ASP.NET Core Filters: Action Filters and Endpoint Filters](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/255-filters.html): Filters run around one action, not every request. Learn ASP.NET Core action filters, how they differ from middleware, and IEndpointFilter for minimal APIs.
- [ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs Tutorial: Routes as Functions](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/256-minimal-apis.html): Build HTTP APIs in ASP.NET Core with minimal APIs: map routes to functions with very little ceremony, on the same framework that runs controllers.
- [ASP.NET Core Controllers and [ApiController] Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/257-controllers.html): Build structured APIs with ASP.NET Core controllers: routing conventions, what the [ApiController] attribute does, and when controllers beat minimal APIs.
- [ASP.NET Core Model Binding: Route, Query, Header and Body](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/258-model-binding.html): How ASP.NET Core model binding finds request values in the route, query string, headers and body, and how to tell it exactly where to look.
- [ASP.NET Core Validation: Data Annotations and FluentValidation](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/259-validation.html): Validate every incoming request in ASP.NET Core with data annotation attributes, and use FluentValidation when a rule depends on more than one property.
- [ASP.NET Core Authentication Explained for Beginners](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/260-authentication.html): Authentication answers one question: who is making this request? Learn how authentication works in ASP.NET Core and how it differs from authorization.
- [ASP.NET Core Authorization: Roles, Claims and Policies](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/261-authorization.html): Decide what an authenticated user may do in ASP.NET Core: role-based checks, claims and policy-based authorization with [Authorize], explained with examples.
- [JWT Authentication in ASP.NET Core: How JSON Web Tokens Work](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/262-jwt.html): How JWTs work in ASP.NET Core: header, payload and signature, why a signed token is readable by anyone, and how to validate bearer tokens correctly.
- [OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Explained for .NET Developers](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/263-oauth-openid-connect.html): OAuth 2.0 lets an app act on your behalf without your password, and OpenID Connect adds who you are. Learn both, and how ASP.NET Core uses them.
- [Rate Limiting in ASP.NET Core: Protect Your API](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/264-rate-limiting.html): Protect ASP.NET Core APIs with the built-in rate limiting middleware, and learn why limits guard against well-meaning clients as much as attackers.
- [Caching in ASP.NET Core: IMemoryCache Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/265-caching.html): Speed up ASP.NET Core by caching expensive results with IMemoryCache. Learn expiration, what to cache, and why cache invalidation is famously hard.
- [Distributed Caching in ASP.NET Core With IDistributedCache](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/266-distributed-caching.html): Why IMemoryCache breaks when you run several instances, and how IDistributedCache gives every ASP.NET Core server one shared cache.
- [Resilience in .NET: Retries, Timeouts and Circuit Breakers](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/267-resilience-fault-handling.html): Handle failing dependencies in .NET deliberately: retries with backoff, timeouts and circuit breakers, and how naive retries cause a thundering herd.
- [Health Checks in ASP.NET Core: Liveness and Readiness](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/268-health-checks.html): Add health check endpoints to ASP.NET Core so orchestrators know when your app is broken. Learn liveness vs readiness, and why one endpoint isn't enough.
- [Observability in .NET: Logs, Metrics and Traces Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/269-observability.html): The three pillars of observability for .NET apps: logs, metrics and distributed traces, what each one can't show alone, and how they work together.
- [OpenTelemetry in .NET: Traces, Metrics and Logs Setup](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/270-opentelemetry.html): Instrument .NET apps once with OpenTelemetry and export to any backend. Learn how OTel builds on .NET's existing primitives, plus auto-instrumentation.

### Part VIII — Enterprise Data

- [Advanced EF Core: Global Query Filters and More](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/272-advanced-ef-core.html): EF Core at production depth: global query filters and other advanced mechanisms for querying and saving data fast, safely and correctly at scale.
- [EF Core Query Optimization: Split Queries Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/273-query-optimization.html): Make correct EF Core queries fast: why including two collections multiplies rows, how split queries fix it, and how to shape exactly what you load.
- [EF Core Compiled Queries: When They Actually Help](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/274-compiled-queries.html): EF Core already caches query shapes. Learn what compiled queries actually save, and the narrow cases where using them is genuinely worth it.
- [EF Core Transactions and Isolation Levels Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/275-transactions.html): Go beyond BeginTransaction and Commit in EF Core: SQL isolation levels, what each one lets other transactions see, and transactions across several saves.
- [EF Core Concurrency Conflicts: Resolution Strategies](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/276-concurrency.html): Catching DbUpdateConcurrencyException is the easy part. Learn the strategies for resolving EF Core concurrency conflicts, with code for each one.
- [EF Core Connection Management and Pool Sizing](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/277-database-connection-mgmt.html): A scoped DbContext doesn't hold one database connection open per request. Learn how EF Core really opens connections, and how to size the pool.
- [Stored Procedures in EF Core: FromSql and ExecuteSql Safely](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/278-stored-procedures.html): Call stored procedures from EF Core safely, and learn which raw SQL methods parameterize your values for you and which ones invite SQL injection.
- [EF Core Bulk Operations: ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/279-bulk-operations.html): Update or delete thousands of rows in one SQL statement with EF Core's ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, skipping change tracking. Trade-offs explained.
- [EF Core Caching Strategies: Identity Map and Beyond](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/280-caching-strategies.html): The caching layers in an EF Core app: the DbContext identity map, IMemoryCache and distributed caches, and the invalidation rules each one needs.
- [Raw SQL vs EF Core: When to Use Each in .NET](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/281-sql-vs-ef-core.html): EF Core or raw SQL? Why both absolute positions are wrong, where EF Core's generated SQL is fine, and when hand-written SQL genuinely wins.
- [Troubleshooting Slow Database Queries in .NET and EF Core](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/282-db-performance-troubleshooting.html): Diagnose a slow database in .NET instead of guessing: make the SQL and its timings visible first, then fix the real cause with the right tool.

### Part IX — Distributed Systems

- [REST API Design Best Practices: The Richardson Maturity Model](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/284-rest-api-architecture.html): Design REST APIs other teams can rely on: the Richardson Maturity Model, resource design, and keeping a contract stable when other services depend on it.
- [Microservices in .NET: Benefits, Costs and Boundaries](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/285-microservices.html): Microservices move complexity from your code to the network. Learn when that trade is worth it, where service boundaries come from, and what it costs.
- [Message-Based Architecture: Asynchronous Messaging in .NET](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/286-message-based-architecture.html): Decouple services in time with messages instead of synchronous calls. Learn message-based architecture and why it reshapes everything downstream.
- [Message Queues Explained: Competing Consumers in .NET](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/287-queues.html): How message queues distribute work: durable storage, explicit acknowledgement, and competing consumers where only one listener ever gets each message.
- [Apache Kafka Fundamentals for .NET Developers](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/288-kafka-fundamentals.html): Kafka is not a queue but a distributed, replicated log. Learn how it retains events and lets many independent readers replay them at their own pace.
- [Event-Driven Architecture in .NET: Events Across Services](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/289-event-driven-architecture.html): Event-driven architecture takes in-process C# events across the network. Learn how services publish facts, how others react, and how to name events.
- [Idempotency in Distributed Systems: Idempotency Keys in .NET](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/290-idempotency.html): At-least-once delivery means duplicates will happen. Learn how duplicates arise and two techniques to make operations idempotent, including idempotency keys.
- [Message Retries and Dead-Letter Queues Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/291-retries.html): Retry failed message handling safely: bounded retries, delivery counts and dead-letter queues, and why retries without idempotency cause harm.
- [Circuit Breaker Pattern in .NET: Closed, Open, Half-Open](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/292-circuit-breakers.html): Stop cascading failures with the circuit breaker pattern: the closed, open and half-open states explained precisely, and how it protects .NET services.
- [Distributed Transactions and Two-Phase Commit Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/293-distributed-transactions.html): Why ACID across independent services is hard, how two-phase commit works, and why it falls short for the distributed .NET systems built today.
- [Outbox Pattern in .NET: Reliable Event Publishing](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/294-outbox-pattern.html): Writing to the database and publishing an event can't be atomic. The transactional outbox pattern makes it one step. Learn how it works in .NET.
- [Eventual Consistency and the CAP Theorem Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/295-eventual-consistency.html): Why distributed systems can't always show the latest write instantly, what the CAP theorem says, and how to engineer around the consistency window.

### Part X — Cloud and Containers

- [Cloud Configuration in .NET: Twelve-Factor Config](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/297-configuration-for-cloud.html): How .NET configuration changes in the cloud: no server to edit, config injected fresh on every start, and the twelve-factor app approach to settings.
- [Docker for .NET Developers: Multi-Stage Dockerfile Guide](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/298-docker-and-net.html): Containerize .NET apps with Docker: what a container really is, and how a multi-stage Dockerfile builds a small, production-ready image.
- [Containerize ASP.NET Core: Ports, Binding and Docker](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/299-containerized-asp-net-core.html): Why an ASP.NET Core app that works locally refuses traffic inside a container, how to bind to all interfaces, and how to build a container-ready app.
- [Environment Variables in .NET: The Double Underscore Rule](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/300-environment-variables.html): Map environment variables to nested .NET configuration keys with the double underscore convention, so container and cloud settings bind correctly.
- [Secrets Management in .NET: Keeping Credentials Safe](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/301-secrets-management.html): Secrets need a higher bar than ordinary configuration. Learn why, and how .NET apps load credentials from dedicated secret stores instead of config files.
- [Kubernetes Health Probes for .NET: Liveness vs Readiness](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/302-health-probes.html): How Kubernetes calls your .NET health endpoints: liveness and readiness probes, httpGet probe configuration, and what happens when a probe fails.
- [Logging in Containers: Structured Logs From .NET Apps](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/303-logging-and-observability.html): Containers have no log files you can tail. Learn how .NET apps should write structured logs in a container and let the platform collect and keep them.
- [Scaling .NET Apps Horizontally: Why Statelessness Matters](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/304-scaling-net-applications.html): Vertical scaling hits a ceiling. Learn horizontal, elastic scaling for .NET apps, and why statelessness is what lets you run twenty instances safely.
- [Cloud-Native .NET: Designing Apps for the Cloud](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/305-cloud-native-net.html): Running in the cloud is not the same as being cloud-native. Learn the design principles that let .NET apps expect failure and scale with the platform.
- [.NET Aspire Tutorial: Introduction to the AppHost](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/306-net-aspire-introduction.html): Get started with .NET Aspire: describe your app's services and dependencies in code with an AppHost project, with orchestration and telemetry built in.

### Part XI — Testing & Prod Eng

- [Unit Testing in C# With xUnit: A Practical Guide](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/308-unit-testing.html): Write unit tests in C# with xUnit, and see how automated tests replace manual checking as your .NET code grows. Clear examples from the first test up.
- [Integration Testing in ASP.NET Core: Test the Real App](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/309-integration-testing.html): Test the real, assembled ASP.NET Core application and catch the wiring and configuration bugs that unit tests can never see.
- [Mocking in C# With Moq: Mocks vs Stubs Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/310-mocking.html): Isolate code under test in C# with Moq. Learn the precise difference between mocks and stubs, and how depending on abstractions makes mocking possible.
- [Testcontainers in .NET: Test Against a Real Database](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/311-testcontainers.html): Use Testcontainers in .NET to start a real database in Docker for your tests, instead of mocks or in-memory providers that hide real bugs.
- [API Testing in .NET: Test the Contract, Not Just the Logic](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/312-api-testing.html): Correct logic doesn't guarantee a correct API. Learn to test status codes, headers and JSON field names in .NET so contract breaks are caught early.
- [Performance Testing .NET APIs: Percentiles, Not Averages](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/313-performance-testing.html): Measure .NET API performance the right way: define a target, generate realistic load, and read latency percentiles instead of misleading averages.
- [Load Testing .NET Applications: Find Your Breaking Point](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/314-load-testing.html): Load test .NET apps to find where they break before your users do: the three common shapes of load test and how to read what they tell you.
- [Debugging .NET in Production: Observe Without Pausing](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/315-debugging-production-issues.html): You can't pause production. Learn how to debug live .NET apps by observing without stopping them and capturing evidence for later analysis.
- [Finding Memory Leaks in .NET Applications](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/316-memory-leaks.html): .NET has a GC but can still leak. Learn the few patterns behind most leaks, especially event handlers, and how to follow a GC root chain to the cause.
- [Diagnosing High CPU in .NET Apps: A Practical Guide](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/317-high-cpu.html): Tell healthy load from a bug when CPU hits 100%. Learn the usual suspects, a step-by-step diagnosis flow, and a real catastrophic regex backtracking case.
- [Diagnosing Deadlocks in Production .NET Apps](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/318-deadlocks-2.html): Find a deadlock in a .NET process you can't step through: freeze the whole picture, read the threads, and tell a deadlock from thread pool starvation.
- [Thread Pool Starvation in .NET: Causes and Fixes](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/319-thread-pool-starvation.html): Every request hangs, but nothing is deadlocked. Learn why the .NET thread pool grows slowly on purpose, how starvation happens, and how to fix it.
- [Database Bottlenecks in .NET: Diagnose Slow Data Access](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/320-database-bottlenecks.html): When a .NET app is slow because of its database: the recurring root causes, a diagnosis flow, and worked examples starting with N+1 queries.
- [Production Incident Analysis for .NET Applications](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/321-production-incident-analysis.html): Five failure modes can look identical in production. Learn a diagnostic decision tree for .NET incidents that rules causes out instead of guessing.

### Part XII — Modern C# 14

- [What's New in C# 14: Every New Feature Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/323-what.html): A guided tour of C# 14: extension members, the field keyword, null-conditional assignment, span conversions, partial constructors and more, with examples.
- [C# 14 Extension Members: Extension Properties Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/324-extension-members.html): C# 14 extension members in full: extension properties, static extension members and the extension block syntax, and what it means for extension methods.
- [C# 14 field Keyword: Field-Backed Properties Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/325-field-backed-properties.html): C# 14's field keyword lets a property add logic without declaring its own backing field. Compare auto-properties, full properties and the new style.
- [C# 14 Null-Conditional Assignment: ?. on the Left Side](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/326-null-conditional-assignment.html): C# 14 lets ?. and ?[] appear on the left of an assignment, so the value is only assigned when the object isn't null. The rules, with examples.
- [C# 14 Span Conversions: Implicit Span<T> Conversions](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/327-enhanced-span-conversions.html): C# 14 adds implicit conversions between arrays, Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T>, making span-based APIs easier to call. What changed and why it matters.
- [C# 14 Lambda Parameter Modifiers Without Types](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/328-lambda-parameter-modifiers.html): In C# 14, lambda parameters can use modifiers like ref and out without spelling out their types. See the before and after, and the rules.
- [C# 14 Partial Constructors Explained](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/329-partial-constructors.html): C# 14 lets a constructor be split into a declaring part and an implementing part, so a source generator can supply the body. How it works, with examples.
- [C# 14 User-Defined Compound Assignment Operators](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/330-user-defined-compound-assignment.html): C# 14 lets a type define += and other compound assignment operators directly, so a += b can update in place instead of creating a new value.
- [C# File-Based Apps: Run a Single .cs File With dotnet run](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/331-modern-file-based-apps.html): Run a C# program from a single .cs file with dotnet run, with no project file needed. Learn how file-based apps work in .NET 10 and when to use them.

### Part XIII — Capstone

- [Designing an Enterprise .NET Application: Capstone Blueprint](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/333-designing-enterprise-apps.html): Start the capstone: design OrderFlow, an order-management system in .NET, from its core entities and services to the constraints it must handle.
- [Clean Architecture Project in .NET: OrderFlow Capstone](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/334-clean-architecture-2.html): Apply Clean Architecture to a real .NET order-management API: what lives in each project, and how placing an order flows through all four layers.
- [Authorization Policies in a Real ASP.NET Core API](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/335-authentication-2.html): Decide endpoint by endpoint what users may do in OrderFlow, the ASP.NET Core capstone API, with real authorization policies and resource checks.
- [EF Core in a Real Project: Repository and Pooling](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/336-database.html): Wire EF Core into the OrderFlow capstone: a real repository, query optimization and connection pool sizing working together in one .NET API.
- [Redis Caching in a Real .NET API: Cache-Aside Pattern](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/337-caching-2.html): Add Redis to the OrderFlow capstone with the cache-aside pattern, and trace a price change end to end to keep cached data correct across instances.
- [Background Processing Pipeline With BackgroundService](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/338-background-processing.html): Run OrderFlow's checkout pipeline with .NET's BackgroundService: one base class, four stages, and an honest look at what this design can't survive.
- [Reliable Messaging With Kafka and the Outbox Pattern](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/339-messaging.html): Close OrderFlow's reliability gap with the outbox pattern published through Kafka, so checkout events survive crashes and reach every consumer.
- [Structured Logging Across Services: Correlated .NET Logs](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/340-logging-2.html): Make one order's journey through five services readable: correlated, structured logging in a real .NET system, stage by stage through the pipeline.
- [Monitoring a .NET System With Business Metrics](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/341-monitoring.html): Go beyond auto-instrumentation: add the business metrics that tell you whether OrderFlow is healthy right now, before any customer notices a problem.
- [Choosing a Testing Strategy for a Real .NET Application](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/342-testing.html): Match each testing technique to what each part of OrderFlow actually risks, instead of applying one kind of test everywhere in the codebase.
- [Containerizing a Real .NET App: Docker Image and Probes](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/343-containerization.html): Ship OrderFlow as a container image a cluster can run, restart and health-check, with one readiness endpoint covering its three real dependencies.
- [Performance Optimization in .NET: Profile, Fix, Verify](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/344-performance-optimization.html): Turn a slow spot on the OrderFlow dashboard into a profiled, fixed and verified improvement, starting with N+1 queries hidden in the hot path.
- [Production Deployment Pipeline for a .NET Application](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/345-production-deployment.html): Take OrderFlow from a laptop to production with a deployment pipeline that enforces what each stage must prove before customers get the release.
- [.NET Architecture Review: Capstone Wrap-Up](https://dotnetmadeeasy.com/Content/346-final-architecture-review.html): A final architecture review of the OrderFlow capstone: step back from thirteen working pieces and check the whole distributed .NET system holds together.
